clinicalPearls: Also called kissing spines, it results from contact and impingement between adjacent lumbar spinous processes
Causes midline axial low back pain that is characteristically worse on extension and relieved by flexion
Most often affects the lower lumbar spine (around L4/5) in older adults with degenerative disc-height loss and hyperlordosis
Tenderness is elicited over the affected interspinous region in the midline
Imaging shows approximation, flattening, sclerosis, and enlargement of the opposing spinous processes, with an interspinous bursa or oedema on MRI
It is frequently an incidental finding, so its role as the pain generator must be confirmed clinically
A diagnostic local anaesthetic injection into the interspinous space can help confirm the source
Management is usually conservative (physiotherapy, postural correction, analgesia, local injection), and surgery such as osteotomy or interspinous procedures is rarely needed
reference.pathophysiology: Baastrup disease arises when adjacent spinous processes come into abnormal contact (kiss) because of loss of intervertebral disc height and increased lumbar lordosis. Repetitive contact in extension produces bony changes, including flattening, sclerosis, and enlargement of the opposing spinous processes, and inflammation of the interspinous ligament, often with formation of an adventitial interspinous bursa. Stimulation of nociceptors in the inflamed interspinous tissues and periosteum generates midline mechanical pain that worsens with extension.
additionalInvestigations: MRI showing interspinous bursitis, oedema, and changes of the opposing spinous processes
Plain radiographs demonstrating approximation and sclerosis of the spinous processes
CT to characterise bony change such as flattening and sclerosis in detail
Diagnostic interspinous local anaesthetic injection to confirm the pain source
Standing or extension radiographs to demonstrate dynamic contact
redFlags: New neurological deficit or radicular symptoms
Constitutional symptoms suggesting infection or malignancy
Severe pain unresponsive to conservative care warranting re-evaluation
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and usually responds to conservative treatment and postural measures; local injections are often helpful, and the rare patient who needs surgery generally does well.
pitfalls: Attributing pain to incidental kissing spines without confirming the source
Overlooking coexisting facet or discogenic pain
Proceeding to surgery without a positive diagnostic injection
references: Resnick: Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: First-line conservative care with activity and posture modification to avoid lumbar extension, plus simple analgesia with paracetamol or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug
Physiotherapy focused on core stabilisation, flexion-based exercises and correction of hyperlordosis
Image-guided interspinous local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Confirm the impinging interspinous level is the true pain generator before intervention, given how often the changes are incidental
Reserve surgery such as interspinous process excision or decompression for the minority with confirmed, refractory symptoms
Refer to a spinal service when pain is disabling or persists despite conservative measures
